# Peer review - Round 1

Reviewers:
- Anonymous Reviewer

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.90164.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.90164.3.sa1)

Summary:

Cincotta et al set out to investigate the presence of glucocorticoid receptors in the male and female embryonic germline. They further investigate the impact of tissue specific genetically induced receptor absence and/or systemic receptor activation on fertility and RNA regulation. They are motivated by several lines of research that report inter and transgenerational effects of stress and or glucocorticoid receptor activation and suggest that their findings provide an explanatory mechanism to mechanistically back parental stress hormone exposure induced phenotypes in the offspring.

Strengths:

- A chronological immunofluorescent assessment of GR in fetal and early life oocyte and sperm development.

- RNA seq data that reveal novel cell type specific isoforms validated by q-RT PCR E15.5 in the oocyte.

- 2 alternative approaches to knock out GR to study transcriptional outcomes. Oocytes: systemic GR KO (E17.5) with low input 3-tag seq and germline specific GR KO (E15.5) on fetal oocyte expression via 10X single cell seq and 3-cap sequencing on sorted KO versus WT oocytes - both indicating little impact on polyadenylated RNAs -

- 2 alternative approaches to assess the effect of GR activation in vivo (systemic) and ex vivo (ovary culture): here the RNA seq did show again some changes in germ cells and many in the soma.

- They exclude oocyte specific GR signaling inhibition via beta isoforms

- Perinatal male germline shows differential splicing regulation in response to systemic Dex administration, results were backed up with q-PCR analysis of splicing factors.

Weaknesses:

- Sequencing techniques used are not Total RNA but either are focused on all polyA transcripts (10x) - effects on non-polyA-transcripts are left unexplored.

The number of replicates in the low input seq is very low and hence this might be underpowered. Since Dex treatment showed some (modest) changes in oocyte RNA effects of GR depletion might only become apparent upon Dex treatment as an interaction. Meaning GR activation in the presence of GR shows changes, upon GR depletion those changes are abolished --> statistically speaking an interaction --> conclusion: there are germline GR effects that get abolished when there is no GR hinting on germline GR autonomous effects.

- Effects in oocytes following systemic Dex might be indirect due to GR activation in the soma. The changes observed might be irrelevant to meiosis and thus in the manuscript are deemed irrelevant, but they could still lead to settle consequences. in other terms.

Even though ex vivo culture of ovaries shows GR translocation to nucleus it is not sure whether the in vivo systemic administration does the same. The authors argue in their rebuttal that GR is already nuclear in fetal oocytes hence the

conclusion that fetal oocytes are resistant to GR manipulation is understandable, at least for the readouts that were considered. Yet the question arises: If GR is already nuclear (active) in the absence of additional Dex treatment why does GR knock out not elicit any changes in the considered readouts -> what are we missing.

This work is a good reference point for researchers interested in glucocorticoid hormone signaling fertility and RNA splicing. It might spark further studies on germline-specific GR functions and the impact of GR activation on alternative splicing.

The study provides a characterization of GR and some aspects of GR perturbation, and the negative findings in this study do help to rule out a range of specific roles of GR in the germline. This will help the study of unexplored options. The authors do acknowledge the unexplored options in their discussion.

The intro of the study eludes to implications for intergenerational effects via epigenetic modifications in the germline and points out additional potential indirect effects of reproductive tissue GR signaling on the germline. Future studies might hence focus on further exploration of epigenetic modifications and/or indirect effects.

claims.claim: Rodent models of gestational physiologic stress can induce neurologic and behavioral changes that persist for up to three generations.
claims.source: Rodent models of gestational physiologic stress can induce neurologic and behavioral changes that persist for up to three generations, suggesting that stress signals can induce lasting epigenetic changes in the germline.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies (Franklin et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2017; Gapp et al., 2014; Franklin et al., 2011; Weiss et al., 2011; Saavedra-Rodríguez and Feig, 2013; Babb et al., 2014; Manners et al., 2019; Bohacek et al., 2015; Gapp et al., 2017; Razoux et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2020).

claims.claim: Treatment with glucocorticoid stress hormones is sufficient to recapitulate the transgenerational changes seen in physiologic stress models.
claims.source: It has been demonstrated that prenatal treatment of rodents with synthetic glucocorticoid stress hormones is sufficient to recapitulate the transgenerational changes seen in physiologic stress models; however, it remains unclear how glucocorticoids are sensed and remembered by developing germ cells (Short et al., 2016; Moisiadis et al., 2017; Constantinof et al., 2019b; Constantinof et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Short et al., 2016; Moisiadis et al., 2017; Constantinof et al., 2019b; Constantinof et al., 2019a).

claims.claim: Glucocorticoid hormones bind and activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR), a ligand-inducible transcription factor.
claims.source: These hormones bind and activate the nuclear hormone receptor glucocorticoid receptor (GR; encoded by the Nr3c1 gene), thus implicating GR-mediated signaling in transgenerational inheritance of stress.
claims.evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GR function.

claims.claim: GR is expressed in fetal oocytes starting at E13.5 and decreasing through E18.5.
claims.source: Female germ cells, identified by either Pou5f1-GFP (Pou5f1-ΔPE-eGFP transgene) or TRA98, showed robust levels of GR starting at E13.5, which waned as development progressed (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: GR consistently localizes to the nucleus of fetal germ cells.
claims.source: GR consistently localized to the nucleus of fetal germ cells, irrespective of developmental stage, suggesting that GR may function as a transcription factor within the female germline (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: GR expression in the female germline decreases from E13.5 to E18.5.
claims.source: These studies confirmed that GR expression in the germline decreased from E13.5 to E18.5 (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: GR is not expressed in adult oocytes of any follicular stage.
claims.source: GR was not expressed in postnatal oocytes between PN5 and PN21, nor in adult oocytes of all follicular stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Female germ cells use a wider range of Nr3c1 exon 1 variants compared to somatic cells.
claims.source: Sashimi plots visualizing the junctions between exon 2 and known exon 1 variants demonstrated that while somatic cells exclusively use exon 1B, 1D, and 1 F, female germ cells use a much wider range of known exon 1 variants, including 1 A, 1B, 1 C, 1D, and 1 F (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data visualized in sashimi plots in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Three novel Nr3c1 exon 1 splice isoforms are expressed exclusively in female germ cells.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we also found evidence of three novel splice isoforms exclusively in the germ cells, labeled here as predicted exons 1α, 1β, and 1γ (Figure 1D, blue lines).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D and validated by RT-PCR in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Genetic deletion of GR does not alter meiotic prophase I progression in fetal oocytes.
claims.source: No significant changes in substage distribution could be detected between WT and KO nuclei, suggesting that loss of GR does not disrupt meiotic progression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by meiotic spread analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Genetic deletion of GR does not change the expression of meiotic genes in E15.5 ovaries.
claims.source: qRT-PCR on E15.5 WT and KO bulk ovary tissue for a panel of genes known to have important roles in meiotic progression similarly revealed no changes in the transcription of meiotic genes (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: There are no statistically significant differentially expressed genes between female WT and GR KO germ cells at E17.5.
claims.source: While our differential gene expression analysis pipeline revealed robust expression differences between WT female and WT male germ cells (Figure 2F and i), we saw no statistically significant differentially expressed genes between female WT and KO germ cells (Figure 2F and ii).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Conditional deletion of GR specifically in germ cells yields no differentially expressed genes at E17.5.
claims.source: Conditional deletion of GR specifically in the germ cells using Pou5f1-CreERT2 yielded the same result (Figure 2F and iii).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Ovarian somatic cells show a robust transcriptional response to dexamethasone treatment (1477 differential genes), while germ cells show a severely dampened response (156 differential genes).
claims.source: While the somatic cells showed a robust transcriptional response following dex treatment (1477 total differential genes with adjusted p-value ≤0.05), by comparison, the response was severely dampened in germ cells (156 total differential genes with adjusted p-value ≤0.05; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Dexamethasone treatment induces PLZF (Zbtb16) expression specifically in ovarian somatic cells and not in germ cells.
claims.source: Fetal ovaries dissected at E14.5 and cultured in hormone-depleted medium for 48 hr with and without 1 μM dex confirmed upregulation of PLZF (Zbtb16, the most highly upregulated gene in the somatic cells by RNA-seq) specifically in the Tg:Pou5f1-GFP– soma and not the GFP+ germ cells (Figure 3B and i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from ex vivo culture experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Dexamethasone treatment does not alter meiotic prophase progression in cultured fetal ovaries.
claims.source: Utilizing the same culture system, we analyzed meiotic spreads and confirmed that dex treatment does not alter meiotic prophase, in line with the lack of transcriptional response (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by meiotic spread analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: GR shows dynamic subcellular localization in fetal oocytes in response to dexamethasone ligand.
claims.source: In ovaries cultured ex vivo without dex, GR localized to the cytoplasm of virtually all germ cells; in contrast, dex-treated cultures retained nuclear localization similar to fetal oocytes in vivo (Figure 3B, ii).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from ex vivo culture experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The truncated GR-D isoform is not detected in E13.5 ovary lysate.
claims.source: We used an antibody designed specifically to recognize all known GR isoforms to immunoblot E13.5 ovary lysate but did not detect any GR-D isoforms (~50 kDa or less), confirming that this dominant negative isoform is not the cause of decreased GR activity in the germline (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: There is no evidence of Nr3c1 intron 8 retention (GRβ isoform) in ovarian germ or somatic cells.
claims.source: However, we saw no evidence of intron 8 retention in our paired-end RNA-seq reads (Figure 3D), suggesting that the GRβ isoform is also not the cause of attenuated GR activity in fetal oocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Male germ cells do not express GR during early sex differentiation (E12.5-E16.5).
claims.source: In stark contrast to the female, germ cells of the fetal testis (marked by Tg:Pou5f1-GFP) showed no GR expression during early sex differentiation (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Male germ cells begin to express GR at E17.5, with over 90% harboring nuclear GR by E18.5.
claims.source: It was not until E17.5 that male germ cells began to express GR, and by E18.5, over 90% of all germ cells harbored GR in the nucleus (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Male germ cells show a pronounced transcriptional response to dexamethasone treatment at PN1.
claims.source: In contrast to the female, differential expression analysis revealed a pronounced transcriptional response in male germ cells following dex treatment, within the same order of magnitude as the GFP– soma (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Dexamethasone-treated male germ cells show enrichment for genes related to regulation of mRNA splicing.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: GR has a sexually dimorphic function in the germline.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Ge et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Full genetic deletion of a single splice factor leads to impairments in spermatogenesis and ultimately infertility.
claims.source: It has been well documented in the literature that a full genetic deletion of a single splice factor leads to impairments in spermatogenesis, and ultimately infertility (Kuroda et al., 2000; Li et al., 2007; O'Bryan et al., 2013; Zagore et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2017; Horiuchi et al., 2018; Ehrmann et al., 2019; Legrand et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kuroda et al., 2000; Li et al., 2007; O'Bryan et al., 2013; Zagore et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2017; Horiuchi et al., 2018; Ehrmann et al., 2019; Legrand et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Spatiotemporal differences in GR expression across different tissues can be due to the use of alternative, non-coding Nr3c1 exon 1 splice isoforms.
claims.source: It has been hypothesized that spatiotemporal differences in GR expression across different tissues can be due to the use of alternative, non-coding Nr3c1 exon 1 splice isoforms in different cell types (Turner et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Turner et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Acetylation of GR by CLOCK results in normal ligand binding and nuclear translocation but complete loss of transcriptional activity.
claims.source: Acetylation of lysines within the hinge region of GR by CLOCK has been shown to result in normal ligand binding and nuclear translocation, but a complete loss of the ability of GR to both activate and repress transcription (Nader et al., 2009), very similar to what is seen in fetal oocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Nader et al., 2009).

claims.claim: Spermatogenesis requires testosterone.
claims.source: given that spermatogenesis requires testosterone (Smith and Walker, 2014), systemic dex administration would not tease apart the cell intrinsic effects of GR activation in spermatogonia.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Smith and Walker, 2014).

claims.claim: Some histone modifications such as H3K4me3 can be transmitted transgenerationally through sperm.
claims.source: While it has been shown that some histone modifications such as H3K4me3 can be transmitted transgenerationally through sperm (Lismer et al., 2020; Siklenka et al., 2015), there is also a growing body of evidence demonstrating that physiological stress leads to changes in the signature of non-coding RNA within the sperm (Gapp et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2020; Gapp et al., 2021; Gapp et al., 2020; Rodgers et al., 2013; Rodgers et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Lismer et al., 2020; Siklenka et al., 2015; Gapp et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2020; Gapp et al., 2021; Gapp et al., 2020; Rodgers et al., 2013; Rodgers et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Physiological stress leads to changes in the signature of non-coding RNA within the sperm.
claims.source: there is also a growing body of evidence demonstrating that physiological stress leads to changes in the signature of non-coding RNA within the sperm (Gapp et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2020; Gapp et al., 2021; Gapp et al., 2020; Rodgers et al., 2013; Rodgers et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Gapp et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2020; Gapp et al., 2021; Gapp et al., 2020; Rodgers et al., 2013; Rodgers et al., 2015).

claims.claim: The regulation of RNA splicing in germline cells is crucial for the proper progression of meiosis and spermatogenesis.
claims.source: The regulation of RNA splicing in germline cells is crucial for the proper progression of meiosis and spermatogenesis (Kuroda et al., 2000; Li et al., 2007; O'Bryan et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2013; Zagore et al., 2015; Naro et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2017; Horiuchi et al., 2018; Ehrmann et al., 2019; Legrand et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021), and is conserved across species (Mattox and Baker, 1991; Wu et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kuroda et al., 2000; Li et al., 2007; O'Bryan et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2013; Zagore et al., 2015; Naro et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2017; Horiuchi et al., 2018; Ehrmann et al., 2019; Legrand et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021; Mattox and Baker, 1991; Wu et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Full body deletion of GR results in lethality at birth due to defects in lung maturation.
claims.source: Because full body deletion of GR results in lethality at birth due to defects in lung maturation (Cole et al., 1995), we generated a conditional deletion of GR in the germline using a transgenic Prdm1-Cre line (Ohinata et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Cole et al., 1995).

claims.claim: The Prdm1-Cre allele causes subfertility in male mice.
claims.source: Control mice containing the Prdm1-Cre transgene, but functionally wild-type for GR (Nr3c1flox/+) showed a significant decrease in the number of sired pups (Figure 6B), consistent with previously reported subfertility with this allele (Mikedis and Downs, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fertility test data shown in Figure 6B and a citation to prior research (Mikedis and Downs, 2017).

claims.claim: Nr3c1 exon 3 deletion results in efficient loss of functional GR protein.
claims.source: Nr3c1 exon 3 deletion has previously been shown to result in efficient loss of functional GR protein (reviewed extensively elsewhere Whirledge and DeFranco, 2018), which we confirmed by IF at E17.5 (Figure 2A), immunoblot at E13.5 (Figure 2B), and qRT-PCR at E15.5 (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence, western blot, and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A-C, as well as a citation to a review (Whirledge and DeFranco, 2018).

claims.claim: GR is a highly modified protein with a wide range of transcriptional isoforms, translational isoforms, and post-translational modifications.
claims.source: GR is a highly modified protein, with a wide range of transcriptional isoforms, translational isoforms, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) described to date (Weikum et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review (Weikum et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Multiple translation initiation sites in the Nr3c1 gene lead to a variety of protein isoforms with varying truncations in the regulatory N-terminal domain.
claims.source: Multiple translation initiation sites in the Nr3c1 gene lead to a variety of protein isoforms with varying truncations in the regulatory N-terminal domain of the protein (Lu and Cidlowski, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Lu and Cidlowski, 2005).

claims.claim: The most truncated forms of GR (the 'GR-D' isoforms) can exert an inhibitory dominant negative effect.
claims.source: The most truncated forms of GR (the 'GR-D' isoforms) can exert an inhibitory dominant negative effect (Lu and Cidlowski, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Lu and Cidlowski, 2005).

claims.claim: In mice, alternative splicing and retention of Nr3c1 intron 8 results in a GRβ isoform that functions as a dominant negative regulator of the GRα isoform.
claims.source: In mice, alternative splicing and subsequent retention of Nr3c1 intron 8 results in a GRβ isoform that functions as a dominant negative regulator of the predominant GRα isoform (Hinds et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Hinds et al., 2010).

claims.claim: In zebrafish, genetic ablation of GR led to accelerated ovarian aging and decline in fertility later in life.
claims.source: In zebrafish, genetic ablation of GR led to accelerated ovarian aging and decline in fertility later in life (Maradonna et al., 2020; Faught et al., 2020; Facchinello et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Maradonna et al., 2020; Faught et al., 2020; Facchinello et al., 2017).

claims.claim: A single-cell RNA-seq study noted that GR expression is highly correlated with progression of fetal oocytes through prophase I.
claims.source: This possibility was raised in a single-cell RNA-seq study of the developing mouse ovary that noted that GR expression is highly correlated with progression of fetal oocytes through prophase I (Ge et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Ge et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Tra2b is a regulator of exon inclusion/skipping known to be expressed in the testis.
claims.source: Both Tra2b (a regulator of exon inclusion/skipping known to be expressed in the testis Grellscheid et al., 2011) and Srsf7 (a member of the SR-rich family of pre-mRNA splicing factors) showed a significant and dose-dependent decrease in expression in response to dex, confirming our RNA-seq results (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Grellscheid et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The theca interna layer is broadly marked by smooth muscle actin (α-SMA).
claims.source: In the somatic compartment, GR was virtually absent from FOXL2+ granulosa cells, but was strongly expressed in the theca cell layer (marked by α-SMA McKey et al., 2020) from as early as PN7 through adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (McKey et al., 2020).

claims.claim: Proper RNA splicing is crucial for meiotic progression in the spermatogenic lineage.
claims.source: As proper RNA splicing is crucial for meiotic progression in the spermatogenic lineage (Kuroda et al., 2000; Li et al., 2007; O'Bryan et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2013; Zagore et al., 2015; Naro et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2017; Horiuchi et al., 2018; Ehrmann et al., 2019; Legrand et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021), perturbations to RNA splicing as a result of elevated GR signaling could have important consequences for fertility.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kuroda et al., 2000; Li et al., 2007; O'Bryan et al., 2013; Schmid et al., 2013; Zagore et al., 2015; Naro et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2017; Horiuchi et al., 2018; Ehrmann et al., 2019; Legrand et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Perinatal dexamethasone treatment increases GR activity in developing prospermatogonia and leads to altered RNA splicing.
claims.source: Our finding that perinatal dex treatment increases GR activity in developing prospermatogonia and leads to altered RNA splicing could confer an evolutionary advantage by increasing the overall transcript diversity of the germline in times of stress, allowing for increased adaptation of the germline to selective pressures from the environment.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing dex-induced changes in splicing factors and splicing events in male germ cells.

claims.claim: Direct activation of GR signaling in male germ cells could lead to alterations in small non-coding RNAs that could be heritable across generations.
claims.source: Distinct from the effects of stress on small RNAs originating from epididymal epithelial cells (Chan et al., 2020), this raises the question whether direct activation of GR signaling in male germ cells could lead to alterations in small non-coding RNAs, and whether such changes could be heritable across generations.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis raised by the authors based on their findings and prior research.

claims.claim: CLOCK could acetylate and inactivate GR specifically in germ cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, our single-cell RNA-seq data shows a strong enrichment for Clock expression in the germ cells in comparison to the soma (data not shown), further bolstering the idea that CLOCK could acetylate and inactivate GR specifically in the germ cells.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation of Clock enrichment in germ cells and prior knowledge about CLOCK's ability to acetylate GR.

claims.claim: Alternative promoters may be cooperatively regulating GR expression in the germline.
claims.source: This wider diversity of Nr3c1 exon 1 variants in the female germline suggests that alternative promoters may be cooperatively regulating the expression of GR, thus leading to the more dynamic temporal regulation of GR seen in the germline in comparison to the soma.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of diverse exon 1 variants in germ cells.

claims.claim: GR may have an upstream regulatory element that is either regulated by a meiotic transcription factor or sensitive to changes in the chromatin landscape induced upon meiotic initiation.
claims.source: We also observed that GR is expressed just prior to the onset of meiotic initiation in male and female germ cells. This suggests GR may have an upstream regulatory element that is either regulated by a meiotic transcription factor, or that is sensitive to changes in the chromatin landscape induced in germ cells upon meiotic initiation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the timing of GR expression relative to meiotic initiation.

claims.claim: Stress is sensed by somatic cells, which in turn elicit epigenetic changes in germ cells.
claims.source: Abundant levels of GR have been identified in the Leydig and peritubular myoid cells of the testis (Stalker et al., 1989; Schultz et al., 1993; Biagini and Pich, 2002; Weber et al., 2000; Hazra et al., 2014), which supports the possibility that stress is sensed by somatic cells, which in turn elicit epigenetic changes in germ cells.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation of GR expression in somatic cells.

claims.claim: It is unclear whether changes in the germline in response to glucocorticoid treatment arise from direct action on germ cells or indirect effects of systemic treatment.
claims.source: While several publications describe a variety of responses of the male and female germline to glucocorticoid treatment (Short et al., 2016; Poulain et al., 2012; Orazizadeh et al., 2010; Ren et al., 2021; Mancini et al., 1966; Yazawa et al., 2000; Mahmoud et al., 2009; Gapp et al., 2021; González et al., 2010; Tohei et al., 2000; Wei et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2016), it is unclear whether such changes arise from direct action of glucocorticoids on germ cells, or the indirect effects of systemic glucocorticoid treatment on hormone production by gonadal somatic cells and/or the hormone producing cells of the hypothalamus and pituitary.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Dex treatment leads to fewer differential splicing events than a full splice factor deletion.
claims.source: We suspect that dex treatment leads to fewer differential splicing events than a full splice factor deletion, given that dex treatment causes a broader decrease in splice factor expression without entirely abolishing any single splice factor.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and comparison to prior literature.

claims.claim: The female germline may have evolved protection against rampant GR-induced transcriptional changes in response to stress hormones experienced during gestation.
claims.source: This is an interesting premise, as it may be advantageous for the germ cells to evolve protection against rampant GR-induced transcriptional changes in response to stress hormones experienced during gestation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about evolutionary advantage based on the observed resistance of female germ cells to GR signaling.

results.result: GR is expressed in fetal oocytes from E13.5 to E18.5 with nuclear localization, but is absent from postnatal and adult oocytes. In the ovarian somatic compartment, GR is absent from granulosa cells but strongly expressed in theca cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 and C29 are well-supported by immunofluorescence data with quantitative analysis (Figures 1A-C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D). The temporal expression pattern is rigorously quantified using computational cell segmentation, and the subcellular localization is systematically documented across developmental stages.

results.result: Female germ cells use a wider diversity of Nr3c1 exon 1 splice variants compared to somatic cells, including three novel germ cell-specific isoforms (1α, 1β, 1γ).
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C9 are supported by RNA-seq sashimi plots (Figure 1D) and validated by RT-PCR (Figure 1E). The identification of novel isoforms is based on paired-end sequencing data and confirmed by independent PCR validation, providing strong evidence for germ cell-specific splicing patterns.

results.result: Genetic deletion of GR in fetal oocytes does not alter meiotic progression, meiotic gene expression, or the overall transcriptional landscape, indicating that fetal oocytes are intrinsically buffered against changes in GR signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 and C30 are supported by multiple orthogonal approaches: meiotic spread analysis (Figure 2D), qRT-PCR (Figure 2E), bulk RNA-seq (Figure 2F), and single-cell RNA-seq (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The consistency across multiple experimental platforms and both constitutive and conditional knockout models provides strong evidence for the lack of GR function in fetal oocytes.

results.result: Dexamethasone treatment induces a robust transcriptional response in ovarian somatic cells (1477 differential genes) but a severely dampened response in germ cells (156 differential genes), with no effect on meiotic progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 are supported by bulk RNA-seq data (Figure 3A), immunofluorescence validation of PLZF upregulation in somatic cells (Figure 3B), and meiotic spread analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). The large difference in transcriptional response between cell types is statistically significant and validated at the protein level.

results.result: GR shows dynamic subcellular localization in fetal oocytes in response to dexamethasone, translocating from cytoplasm to nucleus upon ligand binding.
results.evaluation: Claim C17 is supported by immunofluorescence data from ex vivo culture experiments (Figure 3B, ii). The observation that GR can still respond to ligand by nuclear translocation despite lack of transcriptional activity is well-documented and suggests post-translational mechanisms of GR inactivation.

results.result: The attenuated GR activity in fetal oocytes cannot be explained by the presence of known inhibitory GR isoforms (GR-D or GRβ).
results.evaluation: Claims C18 and C19 are supported by western blot analysis (Figure 3C) and RNA-seq analysis of intron retention (Figure 3D). The authors systematically ruled out known mechanisms of GR inhibition, though the actual mechanism remains unidentified.

results.result: Male germ cells do not express GR during early sex differentiation (E12.5-E16.5) but begin expression at E17.5, with over 90% showing nuclear GR by E18.5. GR expression is maintained in postnatal and adult spermatogonia. GR is also expressed in testicular somatic cells (peritubular myoid cells and Leydig cells).
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C21, and C28 are supported by immunofluorescence data with quantitative analysis across developmental stages (Figures 4A-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B). The temporal expression pattern is rigorously documented and consistent with prior literature on testicular GR expression.

results.result: Male germ cells show a pronounced transcriptional response to dexamethasone treatment at PN1, with enrichment for genes related to mRNA splicing regulation. Splicing factors Tra2b and Srsf7 show dose-dependent downregulation, resulting in 63 significantly altered splicing events (predominantly skipped exons).
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 and C31 are supported by bulk RNA-seq (Figure 5A), GO term enrichment analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), qRT-PCR validation (Figure 5B), and differential splicing analysis using rMATS (Figure 5C). The connection between GR activation and splicing regulation is novel and well-documented through multiple complementary approaches.

results.result: Conditional deletion of GR in the male germline using Prdm1-Cre does not further exacerbate the subfertility phenotype caused by the Prdm1-Cre allele itself, and GR cKO males produce viable progeny.
results.evaluation: Claims C27 and C48 are supported by fertility test data (Figure 6B) and immunofluorescence validation of GR deletion (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). However, the interpretation is complicated by the confounding effect of the Prdm1-Cre allele on fertility, which limits the ability to detect subtle GR-specific effects. The statistical analysis appropriately accounts for this confound.

results.result: GR exhibits sexually dimorphic function in the germline, with female germ cells resistant to GR signaling and male germ cells responsive to GR-mediated regulation of RNA splicing.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 is an integrative conclusion supported by the contrasting results from female (C10-C16) and male (C23-C26) germ cell experiments. The sexual dimorphism is clearly demonstrated through parallel experimental approaches in both sexes, showing fundamentally different responses to GR manipulation.

results.result: Nr3c1 exon 3 deletion results in efficient loss of functional GR protein, as confirmed by immunofluorescence, western blot, and qRT-PCR.
results.evaluation: Claim C49 is supported by multiple validation approaches (Figures 2A-C) and is consistent with prior literature. The validation is thorough and establishes the effectiveness of the knockout model.

results.result: Prior work has established that rodent models of gestational stress induce transgenerational neurologic and behavioral changes, which can be recapitulated by glucocorticoid treatment. Multigenerational paternal stress effects involve glucocorticoid-altered small RNA cargo in extracellular vesicles from epididymal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C33 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for the current study but represent background knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: GR is a ligand-inducible transcription factor that binds DNA response elements and recruits transcriptional cofactors upon glucocorticoid binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C34 represent established scientific knowledge about GR mechanism of action. These are accurate statements of general knowledge that provide necessary background.

results.result: The authors propose several speculative hypotheses: that dex-induced splicing changes may confer evolutionary advantage, that GR signaling in male germ cells could alter heritable small RNAs, that CLOCK may acetylate and inactivate GR in germ cells, that alternative promoters regulate GR expression, that GR has meiosis-related regulatory elements, and that female germ cells evolved protection against GR-induced changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 and C67 are speculative hypotheses proposed by the authors but not directly tested. While some are supported by circumstantial evidence (e.g., Clock enrichment in germ cells for C61), none are rigorously validated. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but should not be considered established results.

results.result: The authors cite extensive prior literature on GR expression in gonads, GR isoforms and modifications, the role of splicing in spermatogenesis, transgenerational epigenetic inheritance, and the effects of glucocorticoid treatment on reproduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C58, C64-C66 accurately represent prior literature with appropriate citations. These provide important context and demonstrate thorough knowledge of the field, but represent background information rather than new findings from this study.

results.result: GR is expressed in fetal oocytes starting at E13.5 with nuclear localization, decreasing through E18.5, and is not expressed in postnatal or adult oocytes.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer describes this as 'a chronological immunofluorescent assessment of GR in fetal and early life oocyte and sperm development' listed as a strength. The editor states the work provides 'convincing evidence' supporting the findings. No concerns were raised about these characterization data.

results.result: Female germ cells use a wider range of Nr3c1 exon 1 variants compared to somatic cells, including three novel splice isoforms expressed exclusively in female germ cells.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer explicitly lists 'RNA seq data that reveal novel cell type specific isoforms validated by q-RT PCR E15.5 in the oocyte' as a strength. No concerns were raised about these findings.

results.result: Genetic deletion of GR (both systemic and germline-specific) does not alter meiotic prophase I progression, meiotic gene expression, or the transcriptional landscape of female germ cells at E17.5.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer notes '2 alternative approaches to knock out GR to study transcriptional outcomes' as a strength but raises concerns about statistical power ('the number of replicates in the low input seq is very low and hence this might be underpowered'). The reviewer also questions why GR knockout shows no effects when 'GR is already nuclear (active) in the absence of additional Dex treatment,' asking 'what are we missing.'

results.result: Dexamethasone treatment induces a robust transcriptional response in ovarian somatic cells (1477 genes) but a severely dampened response in germ cells (156 genes), with no effect on meiotic progression, though GR shows dynamic subcellular localization in response to ligand.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer lists this as a strength ('2 alternative approaches to assess the effect of GR activation') but raises significant concerns: 'Effects in oocytes following systemic Dex might be indirect due to GR activation in the soma' and 'it is not sure whether the in vivo systemic administration does the same' nuclear translocation as ex vivo. The reviewer notes the changes 'might be irrelevant to meiosis...but they could still lead to subtle consequences.'

results.result: Neither the truncated GR-D isoform nor the GRβ isoform (intron 8 retention) are detected in fetal ovarian tissue, ruling out these dominant-negative isoforms as causes of attenuated GR activity.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer explicitly lists 'They exclude oocyte specific GR signaling inhibition via beta isoforms' as a strength. No concerns were raised about these negative findings.

results.result: Male germ cells do not express GR during early sex differentiation (E12.5-E16.5) but begin expressing GR at E17.5, with over 90% showing nuclear GR by E18.5.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer lists 'A chronological immunofluorescent assessment of GR in fetal and early life oocyte and sperm development' as a strength. The editor notes the work demonstrates 'sexual dimorphism in transcriptomic responsiveness.' No concerns were raised about this characterization.

results.result: Male germ cells show a pronounced transcriptional response to dexamethasone at PN1, with enrichment for genes related to mRNA splicing regulation, dose-dependent decreases in splicing factors Tra2b and Srsf7, and 63 significantly altered splicing events.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer states 'Perinatal male germline shows differential splicing regulation in response to systemic Dex administration, results were backed up with q-PCR analysis of splicing factors' as a strength. The editor describes the evidence as 'convincing' and supporting 'GR-mediated alternative splicing in response to dexamethasone treatment in the male germline.'

results.result: Conditional deletion of GR in the male germline using Prdm1-Cre does not further exacerbate the subfertility phenotype caused by the Prdm1-Cre allele alone.
results.evaluation: No reviewer concerns were raised about this fertility finding. The first reviewer acknowledges the study's negative findings 'help to rule out a range of specific roles of GR in the germline.'

results.result: Fetal oocytes are intrinsically buffered against changes in GR signaling, as neither genetic deletion nor agonism with dexamethasone altered the transcriptional landscape or meiotic progression.
results.evaluation: The editor describes this as 'convincing evidence' supporting 'inert GR signaling despite the presence of GR in the female germline.' However, the first reviewer raises concerns about statistical power and notes that 'GR activation in the presence of GR shows changes, upon GR depletion those changes are abolished' suggesting an interaction effect may have been missed. The reviewer questions 'what are we missing' given that GR is nuclear but knockout shows no effect.

results.result: The male germline is susceptible to glucocorticoid-mediated signaling, specifically by regulating RNA splicing within spermatogonia, although this does not abrogate fertility.
results.evaluation: The editor describes the evidence as 'convincing' and supporting 'GR-mediated alternative splicing in response to dexamethasone treatment in the male germline.' The first reviewer lists the splicing findings as a strength with qPCR validation.

results.result: GR has a sexually dimorphic function in the germline, with differential responsiveness between male and female germ cells.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states the work demonstrates 'sexual dimorphism in transcriptomic responsiveness' and describes this as a 'valuable finding.' The first reviewer acknowledges the contrasting responses between male and female germlines throughout their assessment.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on C8-C9 (novel isoforms). Both evaluations find the RNA-seq and RT-PCR validation convincing and mark as SUPPORTED with no concerns raised.
Perfect agreement on C18-C19 (exclusion of GR inhibition mechanisms). Both evaluations find the negative findings well-supported and list as a strength with no concerns.
Perfect agreement on C32 (sexual dimorphism). Both evaluations find this integrative conclusion well-supported, with the editor explicitly calling it a 'valuable finding.'

Strong agreement on C4-C7 (GR expression characterization). Both evaluations find the immunofluorescence data convincing. OpenEval also includes C29 in this group; peer review marks all as SUPPORTED with no concerns.

Disagreement on C10-C13 (lack of GR function in fetal oocytes). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED across multiple platforms. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN due to low statistical power and questions why knockout shows no effect when GR is already nuclear.
Strong agreement on C23-C26 (male germline splicing regulation). Both evaluations find the RNA-seq and qPCR validation convincing and mark as SUPPORTED. OpenEval also includes C31 in this group.

Disagreement on C14-C16 (differential transcriptional response). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED with statistical validation. Peer review marks UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about indirect effects from systemic Dex and potential subtle consequences.
Agreement on C20-C21 (male GR expression pattern). Both evaluations find the immunofluorescence characterization well-supported. OpenEval also includes C28 in this group.

Agreement on C27 (fertility findings). Both evaluations find the data SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes confounding effects of Prdm1-Cre but finds statistical analysis appropriate. Peer review acknowledges negative findings help rule out specific GR roles. OpenEval also includes C48.

Partial overlap on C17 (GR nuclear translocation despite lack of transcriptional activity). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as evidence of post-translational inactivation. Peer review groups C17 with C14-C16 and marks UNCERTAIN, questioning whether in vivo administration achieves same nuclear translocation as ex vivo.

Disagreement on C30 (lack of GR function in fetal oocytes, part of broader claim set). OpenEval groups C30 with C10-C13 and finds SUPPORTED. Peer review evaluates C30 separately as UNCERTAIN, noting 'convincing evidence' but raising concerns about missed interaction effects and statistical power.

Agreement on C31 (GR-mediated splicing in male germline). OpenEval groups C31 with C23-C26 and finds SUPPORTED. Peer review evaluates C31 separately and also finds it SUPPORTED with 'convincing evidence.'
OpenEval finds C49 (knockout model validation) SUPPORTED with thorough validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific methodological claim.
OpenEval finds C1, C2, C33 (background literature on GR and stress) SUPPORTED as accurate summaries. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
OpenEval finds C3, C34 (general GR mechanism knowledge) SUPPORTED as established scientific knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
OpenEval marks C59-C63, C67 (speculative hypotheses about mechanisms) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these speculative claims.
OpenEval finds C35-C58, C64-C66 (extensive background literature) SUPPORTED as accurate representations of prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
